sources.text:
Cornell suspends fraternity parties, gives state police role in investigating campus assault reports
Cornell University is suspending parties and other social events at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year and will give the New York State Police a role in investigating sex crimes on campus, university officials announced Tuesday, amid mounting outrage over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024.
The measures announced by Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff include a suspension of all parties and social events at Interfraternity Council houses through the end of the 2026-27 academic year and a new “zero tolerance” policy for violations that would result in the immediate emergency suspension of a chapter.
“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the campus community.
Cornell has more than 20 active fraternities affiliated with its Interfraternity Council. The council did not immediately respond to an email request for comment.
The university president said the school would begin conversations with students and faculty experts about “the development of safe social alternatives” to Greek life party culture and invest money to get those initiatives off the ground.
He also committed to adding a case manager to the school’s Office of Civil Rights to help those who report sexual misconduct on the Cornell campus navigate the process, and to working with the New York State Police to allow its criminal investigators — who are independent of Cornell — to investigate allegations.
Crimes reported on Cornell’s campus are generally investigated by campus police, a department that has full law enforcement powers but is controlled by the university. The campus police force operates independently from municipal police in Ithaca, New York, where the university is located. Its officers investigated the 2024 gang rape allegations and presented their initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who declined to prosecute within weeks of the woman making her first report to police.
In a lawsuit filed in September, the woman alleged that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members after attending a party at the Chi Phi house in October 2024. She said she was pressured to use drugs and that other men entered the room while she was incapacitated. She also alleges that messages describing her as sexually available to anyone at the house circulated among fraternity members on Snapchat without her knowledge.
Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students following an internal investigation, but no criminal charges have been filed.
New York’s governor removed the district attorney from the case this month after a public outcry over the lack of charges.
The investigation is now being led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, while Cornell has hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct an independent review of the university’s response. New York State Police sometimes handle major crime investigations for small municipal police agencies, bringing in expertise that isn’t available locally.
Kotlikoff’s announcement came a day before Cornell’s faculty senate was to take up a proposed resolution expressing no confidence in the administration’s ability to effectively address sexual assault on campus.
Kotlikoff acknowledged that sexual violence extends beyond fraternities, saying Cornell must also confront a campus culture of excessive drinking and drug use and expand education about students’ responsibility to intervene when others are at risk.
Cornell also plans to add victim advocates and expand sexual violence prevention programs, including education aimed at encouraging bystanders to intervene, he said, calling the various actions announced Tuesday “first steps toward systemic change on our campus.”
“We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors,” he said.

sources.news_title: Cornell Bans Fraternity Parties Amid Gang Rape Allegations
sources.text:
Cornell University has banned parties at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid a reopened investigation into an alleged rape on campus two years ago.
In an Oct. 13 statement, the university’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, said “all parties and social events in Interfraternity Council (IFC) houses at Cornell will be suspended for the remainder of the 2026–2027 academic year.” This, he said, gives “time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue.”
Fraternities that hold in-house parties or events would be subject to an immediate emergency suspension.
Cornell has more than 20 active fraternities affiliated with its IFC. The Epoch Times has reached out to the IFC for comment.
It is unclear whether the new policy applies to off-campus gatherings and events.
That woman, a Cornell student only known as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit on Sept. 16 against the university, the Chi Phi fraternity, and others, alleging sexual assault and negligence. Cornell said that an internal probe led to some students being expelled, other students being suspended, and Chi Phi being kicked off campus. No students were criminally charged.
The woman was “plied with alcohol and drugs to the point of intoxication” at a fraternity house in Ithaca, New York, in October 2024, according to the lawsuit. She was “incapable of consenting” when coerced into taking drugs and forced to participate in sexual acts, the lawsuit stated. She reported the incident to campus police in November 2024.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation into the alleged rape after the suit was filed. The woman went to campus police but did not claim she was gang raped or drugged, he said in a statement on Sept. 28. Instead, she “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.”
“Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” Van Houten said at the time. “I have been asked by the community to revisit the decision whether to pursue criminal charges against the seven fraternity members. I have already begun that process, starting with our conversation with Jane Doe and her attorneys.”
Cornell welcomed the renewed investigation into what allegedly happened. Kotlikoff said the Ivy League school would carry out reforms in response.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor to probe what occurred, removing Van Houten from the case.
The woman went to police and alleged she was raped, according to the governor during an Oct. 2 briefing.
“Yet, shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors,” Hochul said.
Van Houten supported the move and said he would cooperate with James.
Cornell has hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent review of the school’s response.
In his statement, Kotlikoff said there would be more staff to the Cornell Office of Civil Rights, “including the appointment of a dedicated case manager who will help individuals who report sexual misconduct navigate other university processes as needed.”
He also said Cornell is working with the New York State Police to allow their criminal investigators, who are independent of the school, to investigate allegations of sexual assault on the campus.
Cornell will “accelerate the implementation of the recommendations of the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault and expand the scope and nature of the recommendations by engaging the campus community,” according to Kotlikoff.
“These are first steps toward systemic change on our campus,” he said. “We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors.
“Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question.”
Kotlikoff’s statement comes ahead of a faculty senate meeting where members are expected to vote on a measure expressing no confidence in the administration on its handling of sexual assault at the university.

sources.news_title: Cornell University Bans Fraternity Parties over 2024 Gang Rape Lawsuit
sources.text:
Cornell University announced Tuesday that it is banning parties at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year, responding to a former student’s lawsuit alleging she was gang raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
The Ivy League school paired the moratorium with a pledge to add independent sexual assault investigators to its campus police force, according to the New York Times, which reported the changes as the university tried to quiet weeks of uproar touched off by the suit from a woman identified as Jane Doe.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff conceded the school had not done enough in a letter to the campus.
“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” Kotlikoff wrote.
The ban covers all parties and social events at fraternity houses on a campus where one-third of students belong to Greek life, and it lands days before Homecoming weekend. Anne Smalling, the chair of Cornell’s board of trustees, described the step as a reset.
“It’s incumbent on us to try and find other ways for these kids to engage in social settings,” Smalling said.
The university also said it would hire trauma-informed investigators independent of Cornell and add staff to its civil rights office, moves aimed at administrative gaps the Times said were exposed by how Doe’s case was handled. Though campus police interviewed her at length in November 2024, her account was condensed into a six-page summary for the district attorney that left out her statement that she was “100 percent certain” she had been raped.
District Attorney Matthew Van Houten declined to prosecute and turned down a police offer to review more evidence, the Times reported. He reopened the case in late September after Doe sued, and New York Attorney General Letitia James has since taken it over at the request of Gov. Kathy Hochul.
Hochul, James, and Van Houten are all Democrats.
Van Houten has said Doe’s sworn 2024 statement described her drug use and sexual conduct that night as “voluntary, conscious, and consensual,” an account at odds with the lawsuit filed nearly two years later. None of the accused men have been charged, and all deny wrongdoing.
The party ban follows a Cornell Title IX process that, after 12 days of hearings in March 2025, expelled two men, suspended two others, and ordered the remaining three to write “reflection papers.” The fraternity, Chi Phi, remains barred from operating on campus. The faculty senate has given notice of a rare no-confidence resolution against the administration.

sources.news_title: Cornell can do a lot more than pause frat parties
sources.text:
All parties and other social events held in fraternity houses on the campus of Cornell University will be cancelled for the remainder of the 2026-27 school year as the university’s administration contends with a lawsuit alleging a horrific 2024 gang rape in the Chi Phi fraternity house, which has sparked weeks of protest on and off its Ithaca, New York, campus. Michael Kotlikoff, the institution’s president, announced the frat party ban in an email Tuesday afternoon.
“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff said in his email. The university will also be allowing New York State Police to investigate on-campus sexual assault allegations; CBS News obtained a transcript of the interview between campus police and the anonymous student who filed suit against seven Chi Phi members, who told them, among other things, “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped”; campus police reportedly never showed that transcript to the district attorney. The city of Ithaca has also suspended all new Cornell-affiliated event permits, a move that primarily affects fraternities.
Cornell is not the first school to temporarily suspend fraternities or their activities in order to “review” their safety. Three major state universities—the University of Arizona, Louisiana State University, and West Virginia University—have suspended some or all of their on-campus fraternities this month alone amid hazing and assault allegations. (The University of Arizona and Louisiana State University partially lifted their suspensions within weeks.)
In fact, the websites of countless large universities include lists of “suspended or unrecognized” Greek life groups. But the suspensions are typically just that: temporary, and limited in scope. In Cornell’s case, it may be difficult for fraternities to move activities off-campus thanks to Ithaca’s ban—but it remains to be seen how feasible enforcing that ban may be. The same goes for the university’s ban on parties organized by Greek groups on campus.
One study found that fraternity members are three times more likely to rape women than nonaffiliated college men are. Sorority women, meanwhile, are 74 percent more likely to be raped than unaffiliated women on college campuses. But while colleges pause fraternity activities in the wake of hazing deaths, sexual assaults, or other forms of frat-sanctioned violence, they rarely force them to close their doors permanently.
After a fraternity pledge died in a hazing incident at Florida State University in 2017, that university indefinitely suspended all 55 fraternities and sororities on its campus—only to partially lift the ban a year later.
At least a dozen fraternity and sorority pledges have died in hazing incidents since 2020—in that year, given the pandemic’s social distancing requirements, only one young woman died in a hazing incident. That was the lowest number in decades. Most years, multiple students have died.
Abolishing fraternities entirely may be an overdue conversation; the idea seems to come up once or twice a decade. But some schools that have actually moved toward banning single-gender fraternities entirely, like Harvard and Wesleyan University, have backed off in the face of legal threats or suits by alumni.
Where fraternities are smaller, less connected, and less significant in campus life, attempts to ban them have been more successful. Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania banned fraternities in 2019 after leaked messages revealed pervasive misogyny, racism, and sexual violence within its two frats. Middlebury College banned fraternities all the way back in 1991; Amherst College and Williams College have prohibited them since 1984 and 1962.
But in Cornell’s case, Kotlikoff said at a faculty town hall last Monday that permanently banning frats would only make things worse—and could send the problems associated with Greek life “into the shadows.” It’s true that banning fraternities does not automatically eliminate the human capacity for violence. It just takes away a setting in which certain kinds of violence against certain kinds of students are demonstrably made much more likely.

University President Michael Kotlikoff said in a statement that the decision came after listening to the Cornell community’s response to Jane Doe’s allegations that she was coerced with drugs and alcohol before her rape in October 2024 at the now-shuttered Chi Phi fraternity house.

“It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe,” Kotlikoff said. “We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action.”
The decision came after protestors at local rallies in recent weeks have called on the university to ban fraternities, and less than a week after Common Council voted to adopt a moratorium on city permits for all parties and events hosted by student groups.
Jane Doe’s allegations, laid out in a civil lawsuit filed on Sept. 14, quickly drew national interest and set off a flood of criticism of the university for how it initially handled the allegations when they were first raised nearly two years ago.

These and other discrepancies have fueled allegations that Cornell didn’t take Jane Doe’s allegations seriously and have shaken the Ivy League university’s reputation.

Cornell’s announcement said that there will be “zero tolerance for violations” of the ban, with the threat of an immediate suspension for any fraternities that break the new rule. The university had previously suspended its Chi Phi chapter as part of a wave of disciplinary measures against Greek Life in 2024.
In the Tuesday statement, the university promised to work with students and faculty to create alternative social events. It also pledged to hire additional staff to respond to allegations of sexual harassment and assault, including a case manager at the university’s Office of Civil Rights to help individuals navigate the process of reporting sexual misconduct.
The university said it would also expand an interesting effort to address address sexual assault. Cornell released a report on campus sexual assault in March 2026, produced by a task force established in response to Jane Doe’s initial allegations.

University President Michael I. Kotlikoff announced the suspension on Tuesday. It's part of how the university is handling a reopened investigation into an alleged rape at the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024.
In a letter sent to students, Kotlikoff said:
I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community. It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action.
I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni, and trustees, who have shared their feelings of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen at Cornell, and outrage at the broader prevalence of sexual violence against women in our society.
These conversations, and campus protests, have underscored my deep conviction that we must do better: that the time for meaningful and lasting change at Cornell, and at campuses across the country, is now. The independent review led by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates will look at all related Cornell policies and practices, and provide actionable ways that we can improve. However, it is clear that we cannot wait for these findings to take action.
CHANGES AT CORNELL UNIVERSITY
1.) Strengthen Campus Safety -- All parties and social events in Interfraternity Council (IFC) houses at Cornell will be suspended for the remainder of the 2026-2027 academic year. These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue.
- There will be zero tolerance for violations of this directive. Any fraternity holding an in-house party or social event will receive an immediate emergency suspension.
- We will immediately engage students and faculty experts in the development of safe social alternatives and invest university resources in their establishment.
2.) Better Support for Survivors -- We will strengthen our systems of support for survivors of sexual assault in three important ways:
- We will add staff to the Cornell Office of Civil Rights, including the appointment of a dedicated Case Manager who will help individuals who report sexual misconduct navigate other university processes (such as financial aid, academic accommodations, housing, and bursar) as needed.
- We are working with the New York State Police to allow their experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell University, to investigate allegations of sexual assault on campus. These individuals will interview survivors who elect to pursue criminal charges and will prepare comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency. This would be in place for the duration of the independent review.
- Student support staff will be added beyond the Presidential Task Force recommendations to provide additional Victim Advocate support in the Sexual Harassment & Assault—Response & Education (SHARE) office and prevention-focused programs across campus. This is in addition to an existing plan for investment in additional mental health resources.
3.) Changing the Social Culture at Cornell -- Research has shown that campus sexual assault is not limited to the fraternity system. At its core is the specific context of social behavior and a deeply disturbing prevalence of alcohol and drug abuse. While this is not a problem unique to Cornell, we are committed to setting a higher standard for education, oversight, and enforcement of safe social behavior and citizenship.
- We will accelerate the implementation of the recommendations of the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault and expand the scope and nature of the recommendations by engaging the campus community.
- Leaning on faculty expertise in the area of sexual assault and rape culture, and actively engaging and listening to the Cornell community, we will re-form and re-focus the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault on expanded opportunities for safe and healthy social engagement and further ways to reduce risks.
- We will enhance existing education and programming to address the bystander effect and the duty of care we owe each other.
- To provide further support and momentum for this effort, we will engage national sexual violence prevention expertise and community safety organizations to examine the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship.
You can read Kotlikoff's letter and the list of changes at this link.
BACKGROUND
In September, a civil lawsuit by "Jane Joe" accused seven men of pressuring her to consume ketamine and gang-raping her at the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of Oct. 19 and into the early morning hours the next day.
Jane Doe reported the October 2024 incident to Cornell Police in the following days. The university then conducted a months-long investigation into the matter. The university said its investigation led to expulsions and suspensions. The Chi Phi fraternity was also suspended and barred from campus.
However, no criminal charges were filed. The civil lawsuit then followed.
NEW YORK STATE ATTORNEY GENERAL'S INVESTIGATION
On Oct. 2, Governor Kathy Hochul appointed New York State Attorney General Letitia James as the independent special prosecutor in the case. Her appointment comes days after Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said he would present the case to a grand jury.
Van Houten did not pursue charges in 2024. Governor Hochul said AG James was appointed because the case needed a fresh, clean slate.
NO CONFIDENCE VOTE
Cornell University Senators announced on Oct. 6 that they were moving toward a no-confidence vote against the university administration over its handling of the 2024 case.
The committee will review the resolution before it goes before the full Faculty Senate at its Oct. 14 meeting. The resolution would ask faculty to formally declare that they have lost confidence in the university administration. The Senate has more than 75 voting members and serves as the primary legislative, advisory and review body representing Cornell faculty.
A no-confidence vote expresses serious dissatisfaction with an administration and can increase pressure on university leadership to act.
OBAMA ADMINISTRATION DEPUTY ATTORNEY GENERAL
The Cornell University Board of Trustees said it has brought former Obama Administration Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to examine how Cornell University handles sexual misconduct complaints.
The Board of Trustees said Yates assessment will seek to determine how Cornell investigates reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment, what support students get, how the disciplinary process works, campus police responses and oversight of fraternities, sororities and other student organizations.
The announcement was made the same day Cornell Senators announced the plans for a vote of no confidence.
ITHACA'S MORATORIUM
On Oct. 9, the City of Ithaca Common Council approved a temporary moratorium on certain Cornell University-affiliated events that require city permits, using the permitting process to push the university to make changes to how it handles sexual and violent crimes.
The moratorium, which passed 9-1, applies to non-First Amendment-protected activities, including some Greek life parties, sports team events and student organization gatherings that require noise or special event permits.
The council’s action came as city officials pressed Cornell for changes following the sexual assault case involving a Cornell student known publicly as Jane Doe.

sources.news_title: The real power of college has nothing to do with the classroom
sources.text:
Credentials, networks, internships, and prestige keep parents chasing admission even when they think the institutions themselves are disasters.
In the wake of sexual assault allegations at Cornell University, the victimization of women on college campuses has returned to the public conversation.
Cornell’s 2025 state-mandated sexual misconduct survey reported that 35% of undergraduate women said they had experienced sexual assault since arriving at the university. The undergraduate response rate, however, was only 13%. Cornell’s presidential task force itself warned that the low response rate limits estimates and makes the results difficult to interpret.
People will sacrifice their daughters on the altar of the university for status. Imagine what else they will sacrifice.
If you take the headline number at face value, though, sending your daughter to Cornell sounds insane.
Conservative parents correctly tell a parallel story about the ideological and spiritual dangers of college. They complain that universities teach women to hate men, become atheists, sleep around, embrace progressive politics, and borrow enormous sums for degrees of dubious value. Everyone has seen the meme: a smart, pretty, well-adjusted high school graduate goes off to college and returns tattooed, purple-haired, pierced, and wearing a “down with the patriarchy” T-shirt.
Yet both sides keep sending their daughters.
The left describes campuses as rape factories. The right describes them as camps for progressive indoctrination. Still, liberal and conservative parents drill their daughters for the SAT, pack their schedules with extracurriculars, hire admissions consultants, and sweat over essays for the privilege of attending places like Cornell.
And that privilege is expensive. At 2026-2027 rates, four years of tuition at Cornell’s endowed colleges would approach $296,000 before housing, dining, books, and other expenses. New York residents in Cornell’s state contract colleges get a discount, but four years of tuition still comes to roughly $199,000.
Why would parents fight so hard for access to institutions they routinely describe as dangerous?
The easy answer is that neither side believes its own rhetoric. That is too simple. Conservatives and progressives exaggerate, but many genuinely believe the dangers they describe.
The better answer is status.
For most of American history, college was attended by a small minority. It was a finishing school for elites, a pipeline into the learned professions, and an ivory tower for scholars. Most Americans did not need a bachelor’s degree to enter respectable middle-class work.
The G.I. Bill dramatically expanded access after World War II. Federal aid and student lending expanded it further. As attendance grew, the degree increasingly became more than an education. It became a credential.
The Supreme Court’s 1971 decision in Griggs v. Duke Power Co. accelerated that logic. Griggs did not ban aptitude tests, as is sometimes claimed. It held that employment practices with discriminatory effects had to be justified by business necessity and job relevance. Broad employment tests became legally riskier, while a college degree became a convenient screening tool.
RELATED: The ‘Cornell 7’ case should terrify every father of boys
Spencer Platt/Getty Images
That doesn’t mean Griggs single-handedly created credential inflation. It did not. But the larger phenomenon is real. Employers began requiring bachelor’s degrees for jobs that previously did not need them, turning the diploma into a proxy for intelligence, discipline, conformity, and class position.
Eventually the credential became self-reinforcing. A degree was valuable because employers demanded one, and employers demanded one because so many desirable applicants had one.
The result is familiar. Jobs once open to high school graduates now ask for bachelor’s degrees. Jobs once open to bachelor’s graduates increasingly prefer master’s degrees. The education itself may have little relationship to the work, but the credential still sorts applicants.
The economic incentive is only part of it. College has become a rite of passage for the professional class. Parents want the sweatshirt, the move-in photos, the graduation pictures, and the reassuring sense that their children have entered the respectable world. The name on the diploma matters because other people recognize it. The campus experience matters because other high-status people shared it.
A student who attends Cornell does not merely buy classes; she buys membership in a hierarchy that exists long after commencement. This is why attacks on higher education so often fail to change family behavior. Parents can hate the professors, mock the administrators, and denounce the politics while still fearing that opting out will leave their children below the people who stayed in.
College also confers something money alone cannot buy: entry into a social network.
Elite universities connect students with other ambitious, well-connected people. Fraternities, sororities, internships, fellowships, alumni networks, and campus organizations create relationships that can shape careers for decades. Even if every lecture were useless, the network would retain enormous value.
That is why parents who despise universities still want their children admitted to them.
The pressure is especially strong for daughters because women now dominate higher education. Women make up a clear majority of undergraduate enrollment and earn about 59% of bachelor’s degrees. Whatever conservatives may think about the culture of universities, telling a daughter to skip college can mean telling her to surrender access to the credentialed professional world in which many of her peers will compete.
This is the trap.

Blaze Media Illustration
Progressives may believe campuses expose women to unacceptable rates of sexual assault. Conservatives may believe universities corrode faith, family, and femininity. Both groups understand that status institutions control access to other status institutions.
That contradiction reveals something deeper than hypocrisy.
Status is the one commodity that is always zero-sum. People are status-seeking creatures, and institutions that confer status therefore acquire enormous political power. If Cornell can make parents compete for the privilege of paying hundreds of thousands of dollars while those same parents describe the campus as dangerous, then Cornell has something more valuable than an educational product.
It has the power to certify who belongs.
Conservatives spend enormous energy winning arguments about college. They complain about ideology, debt, useless majors, campus sex, and administrative bloat. Then they celebrate when their daughter gets into an Ivy.
That should tell them something.
People will sacrifice their daughters on the altar of the university for status. Imagine what else they will sacrifice.
If conservatives truly want to win the political battle, they should spend less time arguing with institutions that confer status and more time building institutions capable of conferring status themselves.

Cornell students hold dining hall sit-in to call for accountability from university in alleged gang rape investigation
Cornell University students held a protest Wednesday over the school's handling of an alleged gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024.
Students took part in a dining hall sit-in, saying they want more accountability from the administration. They are staging what they call an economic blackout, urging others not to buy anything on campus.
"Student trust in the administration is really low, and that trust only keeps declining as more details of this case are coming out," senior Madeline Gage said.
Gage said students want an independent judicial system established at Cornell, among other demands.
"Additionally, students are hoping that CUPD, our police department, gets proper training on sexual assault awareness, and then, hopefully, that there would be in-person training about consent for students," she said.
Others are demanding major changes within the school administration.
"I would like to see a resignation from our president," student Kiara Videmantay said. "I would call for an end to Greek life on campus or at least some severe reform before we see it opening again."
Meanwhile, the attorney for Jane Doe, the woman who sued Cornell and seven students alleging the assault, says she has been receiving death threats.
"Somebody called her, made a threat to shoot up her house, shoot her, her mother, her father," attorney Thomas Giuffra said. "She's had regular nasty emails calling her names, threatening her. She had one yesterday with three emojis with Colt 45s on them saying she should be killed and things like that."
A spokesperson for Cornell said University President Michael I. Kotlikoff and other members of the administration are set to meet with the Faculty Senate next week. CBS News New York hasn't heard back from the Board of Trustees, which has the final say on leadership changes.
CBS News has reached out to all seven of the men who were named in Jane Doe's lawsuit. We've heard back from attorneys for two of them, who deny the sexual assault allegations.
No criminal charges have been filed.

sources.news_title: What the Cornell case reveals about how sexual assault allegations are handled
sources.text: Anger and backlash are building at Cornell University this week over the way the school handled an alleged gang rape in 2024. The case has renewed questions about how sexual assault allegations are investigated on college campuses and by law enforcement. Geoff Bennett discussed more with Deborah Tuerkheimer, a former prosecutor and author of "Credible: Why We Doubt Accusers and Protect Abusers." Amna Nawaz: Anger and backlash are building at Cornell University this week over the way the school handled an alleged gang rape in 2024. Geoff Bennett: Today, students staged a seven-hour sit-in and launched what they're calling an economic blackout, halting all spending on campus, including with any university operations. That follows a rally earlier this week that drew thousands of students, faculty, and community members demanding justice for Jane Doe, who says she was sexually assaulted by multiple men at Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity two years ago. Saya Taylor, Cornell Protester: Jane Doe deserved an administration that delivered a fair and proper judicial process. Jane Doe deserved a police department that would actually follow up on her case. Instead, she was silenced, her rapists free to walk the grounds of Cornell under a system that chose the university over the student. Geoff Bennett: Yesterday, Cornell announced former federal prosecutor Sally Yates will lead an independent review of the university's handling of the case. And, late last week, Governor Kathy Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James a special prosecutor. The local district attorney did not pursue charges back in 2024. The case has renewed questions about how sexual assault allegations are investigated on college campuses and by law enforcement. Northwestern Law Professor Deborah Tuerkheimer is a former prosecutor and author of "Credible: Why We Doubt Accusers and Protect Abusers." She joins us now. Thank you for being with us. Deborah Tuerkheimer, Northwestern Pritzker School of Law: Thank you for having me. Geoff Bennett: New York data shows that most campus sexual assault cases never reach law enforcement, never result in serious discipline. And yet we know that Jane Doe pursued many of the avenues available to her. There was a Title IX investigation. There was a police report. Of course, there's now a civil lawsuit. When you look at how this case was handled, what should have happened differently? Deborah Tuerkheimer: Well, from the beginning, the criminal investigation really never got off the ground. From what we have been able to tell, there was no effort to build a relationship with Jane Doe. There was no effort to take into account the impact of trauma and the way that traumatic memories are really stored and retrieved and encoded differently than other types of memories. There was very little effort then to gather the kind of corroborative evidence that would give investigators a sense of whether charges were viable. Instead, what we saw is that, from the very beginning, the investigation was dismissed, and Jane Doe was too. Geoff Bennett: And Cornell handled this through Title IX, even though the allegations included serious crimes. At what point should a university turn a case like this directly over to law enforcement? Deborah Tuerkheimer: Well, the choice of whether to take a case to law enforcement really belongs to a victim. In this case, as you said, Jane Doe did seek to pursue both a criminal prosecution and also her Title IX complaint, and that is absolutely within the right of someone who's been the victim of sexual assault. So, often, the proceedings proceed parallel, and they can happen at the same time. One can happen before the other. But, again, here, we saw only the Title IX proceeding go forward, and the criminal case never got off the ground. Geoff Bennett: And New York law has come under scrutiny too, as you well know, over how voluntary intoxication affects sexual assault prosecutions. How does that complicate questions of consent and prosecution? Deborah Tuerkheimer: Well, New York has a provision of its rape law that says that a person who is mentally incapacitated or temporarily unable to control or appraise their conduct due to alcohol or drugs is not able to consent, but only if those drugs or alcohol were administered without the consent of the victim. So that's what's called the voluntary intoxication loophole. About 19 states do treat voluntary intoxication and involuntary intoxication differently. And what it means is that someone who's voluntarily ingested alcohol or drugs is deemed not to be a victim, unworthy of the law's protection. Geoff Bennett: You have written extensively about consent, the skepticism directed at victims, the institutions that can protect the accused. How does the Cornell case fit into that broader pattern that you have researched and written about? Deborah Tuerkheimer: Well, sadly, these dynamics are familiar, all too familiar. And I say sadly, but also maddeningly. In cases across the country every day, victims are met with undue skepticism. They're met with blame. They're met with disregard. I call this the credibility discount, and we see it all the time. It's ubiquitous. Geoff Bennett: And we should say, the names and images of the seven men who have been accused have been spread widely across social media. Their names have, in some cases, been reported, even though none have been criminally charged. And we have seen cases, including the Duke lacrosse case, where men accused of sexual assault were ultimately exonerated. So, what protections are owed to the accused? Deborah Tuerkheimer: Well, in criminal court, the a criminal defendant has the highest level of protection, and that's appropriate because of the consequences that can ensue. And, on campus, there are also protections that are due to a respondent. I think what we're seeing in this case is that the credibility discount means that investigators aren't even doing their job. They're not even pursuing the possibility that a case is viable. And in the Title IX context, all too often, even when a complainant is found to be credible, the sanctions are light and the process is flawed. And so there are so many ways in which the legal system continues to fail accusers in these cases and to provide impunity for abusers. Geoff Bennett: Northwestern Law Professor Deborah Tuerkheimer, thank you again for being with us. Deborah Tuerkheimer: Thank you.

sources.news_title: Cornell Bans Fraternity Parties Amid Gang-Rape Allegations
sources.text:
ITHACA, New York — Cornell University has suspended all parties and social gatherings at fraternity houses for the remainder of the 2026–27 academic year.
The ban is in response to mounting outrage over allegations that a female student was drugged and sexually assaulted by several fraternity members in 2024.
The Ivy League university announced the sweeping restrictions on Tuesday, October 13, alongside plans to involve New York State Police in investigating campus sexual assault complaints and strengthen institutional support for survivors.
Cornell President Michael I. Kotlikoff said the measures would take effect immediately, with any fraternity violating the restrictions facing emergency suspension.
The decision follows weeks of student demonstrations, faculty criticism, and public scrutiny of the university’s handling of allegations brought by a former student identified in court documents as Jane Doe.
The woman filed a lawsuit in September alleging that she was coerced into consuming drugs and sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity during an October 2024 gathering.
Seven former fraternity members are among the defendants.
The men have denied wrongdoing, and none has been criminally charged.
The lawsuit has renewed questions about the university’s disciplinary procedures, its handling of sexual misconduct allegations, and why an initial criminal investigation ended without prosecution.
In his announcement to the Cornell community, Kotlikoff acknowledged the university’s shortcomings and expressed regret over the woman’s experience.
“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024,” he said.
He also acknowledged that women at Cornell continued to question whether they were safe on campus, describing the new restrictions as part of a broader effort to change the university’s culture.
Fraternity Social Life Suspended
Under the new directive, all parties and social events at houses affiliated with Cornell’s Interfraternity Council are prohibited until the conclusion of the current academic year in 2027.
The council represents more than 20 active fraternities at the university.
Cornell has adopted a zero-tolerance policy, meaning any chapter hosting a prohibited event will face immediate emergency suspension.
University administrators said the restrictions would create an opportunity to examine the role of fraternities and determine whether they can continue operating safely.
The review will address not only sexual misconduct but also the broader social environment surrounding fraternity life, including alcohol consumption, recreational drug use, and student behaviour.
Cornell also plans to work with students and faculty members to develop alternative social activities that do not depend on fraternity houses.
The announcement did not establish whether the prohibition extends to fraternity-organised events at off-campus locations.
The restrictions represent one of the university’s most extensive recent interventions in fraternity social life.
In 2022, Cornell temporarily suspended fraternity parties after reports that students had been drugged and a woman sexually assaulted at fraternity-affiliated housing.
The university also introduced tighter fraternity safety measures following the 2019 death of freshman Antonio Tsialas, whose body was found in a gorge after he attended a fraternity event.
Those earlier episodes had already raised concerns about the effectiveness of university oversight of fraternity activities.
Allegations Dating Back to 2024
The controversy centres on events alleged to have occurred during the night of October 19 and the early hours of October 20, 2024, at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house.
According to the civil lawsuit, Jane Doe attended a gathering where fraternity members pressured her to consume drugs and alcohol.
She alleges that she was subsequently sexually assaulted by multiple men while in an impaired condition.
The complaint also describes Snapchat messages allegedly circulated among fraternity members portraying her as sexually available to other men without her knowledge or consent.
The allegations, which have not been established in criminal proceedings, prompted an internal university investigation under Title IX, the federal law governing sex discrimination in educational institutions.
Cornell subsequently closed the Chi Phi chapter and disciplined several students, including expulsions and suspensions.
However, its disciplinary decisions did not result in criminal charges.
Attorneys representing the accused men have disputed the allegations, with some maintaining that any sexual activity was consensual and others denying involvement.
The lawsuit names Cornell, the fraternity, the woman’s sorority, Tri Delta, seven former Chi Phi members, and other defendants.
It alleges that institutional failures contributed to the circumstances surrounding the alleged assault and the university’s subsequent response.
Criminal Investigation Reopened
The handling of the original police investigation has become a central part of the controversy.
Jane Doe reported the alleged assault to Cornell University Police in November 2024.
Campus investigators gathered evidence and referred information to Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, whose office decided not to prosecute.
Van Houten subsequently maintained that the information presented to prosecutors did not establish that a crime had occurred.
However, the woman’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, has challenged the circumstances surrounding that decision.
He told the Associated Press that his client had been given the impression that the investigation remained active when prosecutors had already decided against pursuing charges.
Giuffra also questioned whether prosecutors had reviewed all relevant evidence, including statements about physical violence and messages allegedly exchanged among fraternity members.
The case returned to public attention following the filing of the September lawsuit.
Van Houten announced that he would reopen the investigation, but New York Governor Kathy Hochul subsequently removed the local prosecutor from the case.
Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor, transferring responsibility for the criminal investigation to her office.
James is now overseeing the reopened inquiry.
Separately, Cornell announced on Tuesday that it would work with New York State Police to provide experienced investigators trained to handle sexual assault cases.
The state police personnel will be able to interview survivors seeking criminal investigations and prepare reports for the appropriate law enforcement authorities.
The arrangement is intended to provide an investigative process independent of Cornell’s own police department, whose handling of the original allegations has attracted criticism.
Independent Review Led by Sally Yates
Cornell’s Board of Trustees has also commissioned an independent examination of the university’s sexual misconduct policies and institutional response.
The review is being led by Sally Yates, a former United States deputy attorney general, through the law firm King & Spalding.
Her mandate includes examining how Cornell receives and investigates sexual assault complaints, supports complainants, conducts disciplinary proceedings, works with law enforcement, and oversees fraternity organisations.
The review will also examine the university’s response to Jane Doe’s allegations.
Cornell’s trustees have said they intend to share findings and recommendations with the university community.
However, the scope of any eventual public disclosure remains uncertain.
A Reuters analysis published on Tuesday noted that universities commissioning investigations through law firms sometimes face competing pressures involving transparency, confidentiality, potential litigation, and attorney-client privilege.
The board has not established a public deadline for completion of the review.
Students and Faculty Demand Accountability
The restrictions come after a series of protests organised by Cornell students and supporters demanding greater accountability for sexual violence.
Thousands of students and community members participated in a rally on October 5, while demonstrators organised a sit-in at Toni Morrison Dining Hall on October 7.
Some protesters called for stronger sanctions against students found responsible for sexual misconduct, improved reporting procedures, and greater independence in investigations.
Faculty members have also questioned the administration’s response.
Cornell’s Faculty Senate is scheduled to consider a proposed resolution expressing no confidence in the university leadership’s handling of sexual assault on Wednesday, October 14.
Paul Ortiz, a Cornell professor of labour history and a leading sponsor of the resolution, welcomed the new restrictions but criticised the timing.
He told the Associated Press that the measures had followed sustained student protests, intense news coverage, and pressure from survivors and faculty members.
Ortiz said numerous students, alumni, and university employees had approached supporters of the resolution with accounts of sexual misconduct and concerns about institutional responses.
The proposed no-confidence resolution represents a significant test of confidence in Kotlikoff’s leadership, although it does not itself constitute a decision to remove him.
The controversy has also reached beyond the campus.
On October 8, hundreds of demonstrators gathered in New York City under the banner of an emerging movement against sexual violence, drawing attention to the Cornell allegations and broader concerns about accountability.
Survivor’s Lawyer Welcomes Changes but Says They Came Too Late
Giuffra said the measures announced by Cornell represented progress but could not undo what his client had experienced.
In comments to NBC News, he said Jane Doe had pursued litigation partly to improve how the university responds to allegations of abuse.
He welcomed the new initiatives but said they had come too late to protect her.
The lawyer expressed hope that the changes would prevent similar experiences among future students.
The Cornell president has also announced plans to increase staffing at the university’s Office of Civil Rights, appoint a dedicated case manager to assist students reporting sexual misconduct, and expand prevention education and victim advocacy services.
The proposed support arrangements will help complainants navigate academic accommodations, housing arrangements, financial aid, and other university processes while their cases are reviewed.
Kotlikoff has said the university must address the prevalence of excessive drinking and drug use, as well as the responsibility of students to intervene when they witness potentially dangerous situations.
He acknowledged that sexual violence is not confined to fraternities and that any lasting institutional reform must extend beyond restricting fraternity social events.
For Cornell, the immediate challenge is implementing the new restrictions while the criminal investigation, civil litigation, faculty scrutiny, and independent institutional review continue.
Whether the university ultimately restores fraternity social events will depend on the outcome of its broader examination of campus safety and fraternity life.

sources.news_title: Cornell’s Fraternity Party Ban: Too Little, Too Late—and Too Easy to Evade
sources.text:
Cornell University has suspended fraternity-house parties for the remainder of the academic year in response to outrage over allegations that a former student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity in 2024. The measure is sweeping in appearance. Whether it will make women safer is another question.
President Michael Kotlikoff announced Tuesday that parties and social events at houses belonging to Cornell’s Interfraternity Council are prohibited through the end of the 2026–27 academic year. Fraternities that violate the suspension face immediate emergency suspension of their chapters. The university will also involve New York State Police in campus sex-crime investigations and has commissioned an independent review of its handling of sexual misconduct allegations.
“It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe,” Kotlikoff said. “We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action.”
The additional measures could have consequences beyond the immediate controversy. The party ban, however, has an obvious weakness: It targets where fraternity events take place, not necessarily the people organizing them.
Fraternities could move their parties to members’ apartments, rented houses or other off-campus locations. This is not merely speculation. When Cornell temporarily suspended Greek-sponsored events in 2022, some fraternities moved their parties off campus.
If the new prohibition is enforced only at fraternity houses, the university risks repeating the same exercise: announcing a crackdown, disrupting the social calendar and leaving the underlying behavior largely untouched.
Cornell has disciplinary tools that extend beyond fraternity property. The question is whether it will use them to hold chapters accountable when they relocate events or organize parties through unofficial channels. The university has yet to demonstrate how it will close that loophole.
A ban cannot substitute for accountability
The immediate trigger for Cornell’s action was a civil lawsuit filed in September by a former student identified as Jane Doe. She alleges that seven men sexually assaulted her over several hours at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024 after she became incapacitated by drugs and alcohol. The allegations have not resulted in criminal convictions.
In testimony to a university hearing panel, Doe described herself as having been “prostituted” and “held up like bait for a gaggle of men.” She pleaded with the panel to “make Cornell a better and safer place” by removing the men she accused from campus.
Cornell closed the Chi Phi chapter and imposed disciplinary sanctions. Two men were expelled, while others received lesser penalties, including suspensions and educational assignments. The disparity between those sanctions and the seriousness of the allegations helped fuel criticism of the university’s response.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the case. Former acting U.S. attorney general Sally Yates will independently review Cornell’s handling of the allegations and its broader sexual-misconduct policies.
These investigations may prove more consequential than the party ban because they address how allegations are investigated, how disciplinary decisions are made and whether those responsible are held accountable.
Moving a party does not eliminate the possibility of sexual assault, just as closing a fraternity house does not eliminate predatory behavior. A meaningful response requires enforcement that follows the organizers, credible investigations, support for survivors and consequences proportionate to established misconduct.
The test comes after the announcement
Cornell says the suspension will give it time for “a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue.” But the university has previously introduced restrictions and reforms intended to improve fraternity safety. The 2024 allegations emerged despite those efforts.
The new policy may be a necessary immediate response to a crisis of confidence. It is not, by itself, evidence that the crisis has been addressed.
Cornell must show that it can enforce its rules beyond fraternity property lines, investigate allegations without the appearance of institutional self-protection and make clear that membership in a powerful social organization offers no shield from accountability.
Otherwise, the university will have achieved something visible but limited: parties may disappear from fraternity houses while the conditions that prompted the ban remain intact.
The measure of success will not be how many parties Cornell cancels. It will be whether the university changes what happens when a student reports sexual assault—and what consequences follow.

sources.news_title: Cornell Fraternity Party Ban: New Campus Safety Changes
sources.text:
The university pauses IFC house social events and seeks outside investigators as scrutiny of its response to a 2024 assault allegation continues.
Cornell’s fraternity party ban takes effect immediately and runs through the end of the 2026–27 academic year. President Michael I. Kotlikoff announced October 13 that parties and social events in Interfraternity Council houses are suspended while Cornell examines fraternity life and strengthens its response to sexual assault. This significant decision reflects a broader commitment to safety in light of the Cornell fraternity party ban.
The changes follow renewed scrutiny of allegations involving a former student identified publicly as Jane Doe. They raise questions that reach beyond Ithaca: Who investigates a campus assault report, who supports the student, and how can families assess whether a college’s promises become practice?
What does Cornell’s fraternity party ban cover?
According to Cornell’s announcement, violating the IFC house restriction brings immediate emergency chapter suspension. Cornell will fund safer social alternatives.
Other measures include:
- A civil-rights case manager to help reporting students navigate financial aid, academics, housing and billing.
- Work with independent New York State Police investigators during the external review.
- Added victim advocates, prevention programming and mental-health investment.
- Faster task-force reforms, stronger bystander education and outside prevention expertise.
State Police investigators would interview survivors choosing a criminal process and prepare summaries for law enforcement. Cornell will also refocus its sexual-assault task force on safer social life.
“Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question,” Kotlikoff wrote.
Why is the university under scrutiny?
The Associated Press reported that the announcement comes amid anger over Cornell’s handling of a woman’s allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity house in 2024. The policy response should not be confused with a criminal verdict.
Jane Doe’s civil allegations remain allegations. Reporting them accurately means taking the complaint seriously while preserving the rights of those accused. An investigation, a university sanction and a court judgment answer different questions. None should be casually treated as a substitute for another.
Attorney general’s investigation is a separate process
On October 1, the New York attorney general’s office confirmed that Governor Kathy Hochul appointed it special prosecutor to investigate the alleged October 2024 assault at Cornell.
“Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly,” Attorney General Letitia James said.
That appointment concerns the alleged incident. Cornell’s broader policy review concerns the institution’s systems. Readers should watch each process on its own terms, without assuming that a finding in one automatically determines the outcome of the other.
What will Sally Yates’ independent review examine?
Cornell’s trustees announced October 6 that former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Q. Yates, now a King & Spalding partner, will lead an independent review. It includes a detailed examination of Cornell’s response to Jane Doe’s allegations involving Chi Phi members in October 2024 and whether Cornell followed its own rules.
The wider inquiry covers reporting, investigations, student support, hearings, discipline and appeals. It also examines campus police, coordination with prosecutors, safety reporting, student-organization oversight and the board’s own oversight.
Yates’ team will assess practices against applicable federal and state requirements and recognized prevention practices. Cornell says the team will have access to relevant records and personnel, subject to law and privacy protections. Findings go directly to the trustees’ special committee. The board intends to share results and recommendations with the Cornell community.
The announcement gives no firm completion date. Trustees requested a review that is both prompt and thorough.
Why this matters to Mohawk Valley families
For students and parents considering any college, the useful response is to ask concrete questions. A polished safety brochure is a starting point. Ask the school to explain how help actually works when a student is frightened, uncertain or unable to continue normal coursework.
- Identify confidential help. Ask which staff can discuss options privately and what limits apply.
- Map the reporting paths. Request an explanation of school procedures and law-enforcement options.
- Ask about practical support. Find out who handles housing concerns, missed classes and other urgent needs.
- Check accountability. Ask how students receive updates and where they can raise concerns about the process.
These are questions for every institution. This report does not establish that a Mohawk Valley college shares Cornell’s problems.
New York already has a campus-safety framework
The state’s Enough is Enough program, established in 2015, addresses campus sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence and stalking. Its requirements include comprehensive college procedures, a uniform affirmative-consent definition, a student bill of rights, reporting-related amnesty, campus climate surveys and prevention training.
The Office for the Prevention of Domestic Violence says its funding program supports 52 rape crisis programs. Services include advocacy, counseling, case management and safety planning, alongside prevention work.
The state lists YWCA of the Mohawk Valley as a provider for Oneida and Herkimer counties. It lists Liberty Resources’ Help Restore Hope Center for Madison County. Students can use the state’s provider directory to identify support near home or school.
Where students and families can find support
Cornell’s SHARE office offers victim advocacy and prevention services for its community. Its website directs readers to information on getting care, reporting, helping a friend and participating in prevention efforts. The office can be reached at share@cornell.edu, or through 607-255-4782.
Nationally, RAINN’s National Sexual Assault Hotline connects people with trained support specialists around the clock. Call 800-656-HOPE (4673), text HOPE to 64673, or use its online chat.
RAINN offers confidential support and referrals for local services, medical or legal needs, and longer-term care. People need not provide identifying information. Its published policy explains reporting obligations that can apply if a caller shares identifying details and is a minor or vulnerable adult. Review those terms if privacy is a concern.
Related coverage: Hochul names attorney general special prosecutor in Cornell assault case.
What should readers watch next?
The key questions now concern implementation: when promised staff begin work, how students access outside investigators, what the independent review finds, and how recommendations translate into measurable changes.
Families can use this moment to locate support contacts before a crisis occurs. Save the relevant campus and community resources, and share those links with a student who may need them.

sources.news_title: Handling of rape allegations at Cornell shows why so many assaults go unreported – victims don’t trust the institutions that are supposed to help them
sources.text:
by Kaitlyn M. Sims, University of Denver; Institute for Humane Studies, [This article first appeared in The Conversation, republished with permission]
The drinking, drugging and sexual assault culture on American college campuses is once again attracting national attention.
A former Cornell University student filed a civil lawsuit in September 2026 alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members gang-raped her when she was a sophomore at the school two year earlier.
The apparent failure of institutions she reached out to for help has become an important part of the story.
As a researcher who studies domestic and sexual violence – and as a college professor who works with students every day – the unfolding narrative about the so-called “Cornell 7” has weighed on me.
Estimates of student sexual assault often understate the problem. Many students do not report an assault because they don’t know where to turn, have concerns about confidentiality, don’t trust the university to respond adequately or are unable to navigate the institution’s resources by themselves.
This parallels vast underreporting of sexual assault and abuse in general.
Sexual violence reporting on campus
The response by Cornell and Ithaca, N.Y., police underscores what many victims of sexual violence nationwide fear about reporting their assaults to authorities.
Only 37.5% of surveyed college students believed campus officials will take seriously sexual assault allegations when physical force or an inability to consent is involved – as was allegedly the case for Jane Doe. Only 7.1% of surveyed students who were assaulted contacted local police.
In Jane Doe’s case, she reported the assault to police three weeks after it took place. Despite telling police definitively that she had been raped, the report Ithaca police sent to the district attorney omitted this language.
The district attorney in the county where Cornell is located declined to press charges against any of the seven men who were accused of involvement in the assault – without ever conducting an interview with Jane Doe.
The school’s own internal investigation led to two of the alleged perpetrators being expelled, two more being suspended and a fifth who had already graduated being barred from campus. The other two students were required to attend training, avoid contact with Jane Doe and write reflection essays.
After Doe’s lawsuit was filed, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to investigate how campus and local authorities handled the case.
Understanding where students are at risk
While campus sexual assault is a well-known issue, data on the current state of the problem is limited.
Under the 1990 Clery Act, federally funded colleges must report annual crime and safety data, but these include sexual assaults only if they are formally reported. Since only 16% of victims report their assault through formal channels, this dramatically undercounts students’ experiences of campus sexual assault.
Large private surveys of students at multiple colleges consistently estimate that 1 in 5 college women are assaulted while attending university. Risks are higher for students involved in fraternities or sororities, like Jane Doe and her alleged assailants were.
Counter to the popular perception that perpetrators are unknown assailants, most sexual assaults are perpetrated by someone known to the victim, and over 21% are committed by an intimate partner. In the case at Cornell, Jane Doe went to the Chi Phi house specifically to meet a friend who then allegedly participated in the assault.
Alcohol and other drug use creates an especially high risk for sexual assault. Campus climate surveys show that a majority of surveyed students who were assaulted had voluntarily consumed alcohol and other drugs before the assault happened. Jane Doe reported being incapacitated and “near hallucinating” due to ketamine and alcohol during the incident.
Effects of assault can last for years
College sexual assault impacts students far beyond graduation.
Students who are sexually assaulted are at higher risk for reporting anxiety and depression. Adverse mental and physical health effects of college sexual assault can last for years after graduation. Students who are assaulted are more likely to have lower grades and learning difficulties – or drop out of college altogether, as Jane Doe did.
Schools receiving federal funding have a legal obligation under Title IX to respond to allegations of sexual assault and sexual harassment. This 1972 federal law prohibits sex-based discrimination in education programs, including on college campuses.
Given the scale of campus sexual assault, many campuses have adopted new programs to try to reduce assaults on campus.
Web-based interventions and small-group intensives can reduce victimization, improve students’ self-defense measures, and improve bystander intervention awareness. Bystander intervention training teaches students to safely step in when they see unsafe behavior.
These programs help students change their behaviors, such as reducing binge drinking, and combat pervasive “rape myths,” or the belief that victims of sexual assault were “asking for it.”
But the focus remains on teaching potential victims how to defend themselves and look out for their peers. Researchers know much, much less about interventions that can prevent people from perpetrating sexual assaults.
Policies could support victims
Gov. Hochul has already called out a “loophole” in the New York law that may have impacted Jane Doe’s case.
Under New York state law, sexual contact with someone who is “mentally incapacitated” due to drugs or alcohol is only rape if the victim was involuntarily intoxicated, such as in the case of “roofie”-facilitated assaults. Because Jane Doe voluntarily consumed alcohol before arriving at the Chi Phi house and knowingly took ketamine, the alleged gang rape may not be considered to be legally a crime. Hochul has said that she will work to close the loophole, as “voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape.”
Other changes in New York have already improved support systems available for victims. As of 2026, the state no longer requires police reports for crime victims to access state compensation funds that can be used to reimburse victims for crime-related expenses like hospital bills, mental health counseling and lost wages. Victims of sexual violence who are worried that police may not believe them can have their crime verified by a victim service agency or a mental or physical health professional. They now also have up to three years after the crime is reported to file for compensation, up from a former one-year time limit.
These funds, which exist in every state, can help survivors work to reestablish their lives after violence. But most survivors don’t receive crime victim compensation.
In Illinois, fewer than 20% of compensation claims by sexual assault victims were paid out between 2015 and 2020. A 2022 national survey found that 96% of victims of violent crime who were surveyed did not receive crime victim compensation.
Other states have yet to revise their compensation programs to account for the specific needs of victims of sexual assault. In Colorado, where I teach, the state didn’t remove a requirement that victims report the crime to police within 72 hours until 2024. Victims do still need to report to police unless they receive a forensic sexual assault exam, known as a “rape kit” – a particularly frustrating requirement in a state that only recently had a 517-day wait for kits to be processed.
And in some states, victims seeking compensation can receive reduced payouts or be denied outright if they were involved in conduct that “contributed” to their victimization. For victims of campus sexual assault, this can include having consumed illegal drugs or alcohol while underage. In Alabama, drug and alcohol use that led to “poor judgment” by the victim is grounds for denial of compensation, and Arkansas denies any victim who was using drugs at the time of the crime.
The result is that many survivors of campus sexual assault may find themselves excluded from the systems meant to help them when they report. And the current news about the Cornell 7 is likely to further fracture students’ confidence in reporting future assaults altogether.
If you or someone you know has been affected by sexual assault, help is available. The Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN) operates a 24/7 helpline at 800-656-HOPE. Victims of violence in New York can receive assistance from the state’s Office of Victim Services.
Portions of this article originally appeared in a previous article published on Sept. 3, 2026.
Kaitlyn M. Sims, Assistant Professor of Public Policy, University of Denver; Institute for Humane Studies
