sources.news_title: Calls for accountability in a time of confusion
sources.text:
By: Lily Sawyers and Autumn Reeves, Freelance Reporters
The recent sexual assault case at Cornell University has left many people with more questions than answers, particularly about what repercussions happen after a student decides to report.
In October 2024, a Cornell student, publicly identified as Jane Doe, reported an alleged sexual assault at the university’s Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York. The university investigated the allegations through its Title IX and disciplinary processes, eventually imposing sanctions against several of the students involved.
Now nearly 2 years later, the case is still unfolding. The criminal investigation has been reopened, and New York Attorney General Letitia James has been appointed as a special prosecutor.
This case has drawn renewed attention to a different question for universities: What does it really mean to protect a student if the support ends after they report? When any student reports sexual assault to their university, the bare minimum should be that they feel like someone is going to truly help them.
Title IX is supposed to provide students with a way to report sexual misconduct and receive support. Having a policy, reporting systems, or a list of resources is one thing, but making a student feel supported after they choose to use those resources is a different story.
Social media has been a catalyst for the opinions of those who both want change and those who oppose Title IX.
Autumn:
When it comes to the sexual assault case that has been taking over the news, I have many thoughts that a majority of people would agree on. However, there are a few things that I don’t see many people bring up. One such thing is Title IX.
Many people, especially college students, have heard about Title IX or were required to learn about it. Despite that, a lot of people still don’t understand how it works.
Title IX was a civil rights law passed in 1972, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sex. Along with this, the law prohibits sexual harassment, sexual assault, dating violence, and stalking, among other things.
Here at Ferris, Title IX is alive and well. Students are encouraged to report cases, and emergency phones are stationed around campus, noticeable by their blue lights.
But how helpful is Title IX? Does it really protect students or make them comfortable enough to open up about the things they’ve experienced? I would say no.
On the outside, it looks like universities care, have your best interests in mind, and want to ensure that you can be a college student without fear of others. However, I’ve seen the way people’s cases are handled, and I believe that this isn’t true.
Though Title IX sounds like it would be helpful, it relies solely on the way the university handles situations.
For example, Cornell’s Title IX investigated Jane Doe’s assault in detail, looking into everything she said she went through. Yet barely anything happened. Title IX held on to the information gathered through the investigation, and for some reason, did not use it to its full potential.
Two students were expelled, the Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, five other students were required to write essays to the administration, and the rest of the fifty Chi Phi members in the Snapchat group–who saw what was happening–went away scot-free.
Jane Doe never got to graduate, and the alleged assaulters were never convicted of their crimes.
How is this possible? If the police were contacted, if the evidence was there, how was there no trial? Most importantly, why was Jane Doe not given the resources to feel comfortable on campus?
I believe there need to be more resources for students who choose to utilize Title IX. They don’t need help recalling their experiences; they need help finding a path forward. They need help getting justice.
Their problems have been brushed away for various reasons. Maybe they don’t feel comfortable sharing everything, and the university doesn’t see it as an actual case. Maybe the university doesn’t want to damage the reputation of an alleged offender. In these instances, the perpetrator receives more support than the victim. Something has to change.
University campuses deserve to be a place of learning. Students deserve to feel safe and comfortable. I believe that we can be the change we’re looking for.
Instead of ignoring problems or putting up a facade that students are being cared for, I believe we need to actually lead students to the help they need. Victims need to be heard; they need to have the resources to speak up.
Whether that be through a trial or accountability for those who choose to harm others, Title IX needs to account for more than just the beginning of a victim’s story. Now is the time to make sure that students can rely on people who have the means to help them.
Lily:
What is most vile about this case is that the student who came forward with the alleged sexual assault has spent years waiting for answers and accountability. Cornell’s disciplinary processes and the criminal investigations are separate, but that does not make the length of this process any less concerning.
The responsibility extends beyond the seven men named in the lawsuit. Reports about the Snapchat group– which involved approximately 57 members– raise questions about the responsibility of those who witnessed discussions about the incident.
Accountability should not stop with the people accused.
What disciplinary actions are being assigned to the people who knew about it and did nothing to help? What are fraternities doing to ensure their members understand that remaining silent and looking the other way is never acceptable? Universities cannot claim to prioritize student safety while leaving these questions unanswered.
As national attention grew, social media became another place where people began demanding answers and showing support for Jane Doe. The “I am Jane Doe” trend shows the solidarity of women who claim the name to make it more difficult to identify the victim.
The case has also sparked conversations about sexual assault as a whole, including how important it is to make those who committed that crime accountable for their actions, even if they were bystanders.
At the same time, misinformation, just like in any other story, is circulating online, showing how quickly social media can blur the line between facts and speculation. Social media may have amplified the story, but we must remember that the facts of the case do not change, and neither do questions about accountability.
Every student deserves more than just policies on paper. We deserve to know that we can speak up. The Cornell case should remind universities and fraternities that their responsibility does not end when a report is filed.
Title IX can provide us with a path for students to come forward, but that path means little if it is not enforced. If we as a nation are serious about creating safer campuses, accountability cannot begin only when pressure becomes a factor. It has to start right away with the institutions and communities responsible for protecting their students.

sources.news_title: Students add campus safety to the college application checklist
sources.text:
A reopened investigation into a 2024 sexual assault allegation at Cornell University has reemphasized campus safety as students apply to college.
A former Cornell student filed a lawsuit in early September this year against the university, alleging she had been sexually assaulted during a fraternity party.
The lawsuit drew renewed scrutiny, particularly after some of those accused were suspended but allegedly told they could return if they wrote an essay. Cornell denied the allegations, according to a statement by Kyle Kimball, the university’s vice president for university relations.
The case has also prompted high schoolers to reconsider how much they know about the safety of the colleges they are applying to.
“I assumed that most of the schools were going to be a secure, safe campus,” said Sienna Massabki, a senior at Carlmont High School who has applied to around a dozen colleges.
In 2025, Cornell conducted a study and found that 35% of their undergraduate women experienced nonconsensual sexual contact during their time at Cornell, up from 23% two years prior.
For students like Massabki, however, campus safety is rarely as simple as checking a criminal incident report. Each college reports different types of incidents and uses different disciplinary processes, making it difficult for applicants to equate a number with their potential experience on campus.
Students consider how safe they feel in their day-to-day lives, both on and off-campus, how universities respond when sexual misconduct is reported, and whether a school’s reputation or opportunities could outweigh concerns about campus safety.
“The best way to get a real grasp of safety is to talk to someone on campus,” said Vania Pala, a Carlmont alumna and current student at the University of California, Berkeley.
According to Pala, Berkeley students receive frequent safety reports through the university’s official WarnMe system. Over time, repeated notifications about nearby crime have become less alarming and more a matter of preparation.
However, she said that even though Berkeley has systems for reporting incidents, it can be difficult to see where reports go after they are made and what disciplinary measures, if any, follow.
As a result, she said, students can feel that much of the responsibility falls on them to avoid potentially unsafe situations. Fraternity houses and other social settings are particularly difficult places to navigate for prospective students.
“Even I don’t think I knew anything about it before coming to college,” Pala said.
According to Kieron Narth, a Carlmont senior, the uncertainty of what happens after a report is filed can affect where students are willing to apply in the first place.
“I have kind of rethought about applying to universities like Stanford, or other Ivy League schools, because it shows how I really have to consider where in the country I am,” Narth said.
Narth initially focused more on factors such as academics when considering colleges. The Cornell case made him think more about the location’s safety and how much safety information prospective students can find before enrolling.
“I wish that I had known more about sexual assault cases on college campuses instead of just assuming that every campus is going to be okay, even if it’s an Ivy League school,” Narth said.
Others said that reconsidering a school isn’t always as simple as removing it from a list.
Kaitlin Hsu, an Aragon High School senior, considered applying to Cornell because of its architecture program. After learning more about the sexual assault allegations and the university’s response, she decided not to complete the application.
Hsu said students can become focused on programs and reputation without considering what their day-to-day experience on campus might be.
“They see the numbers, but they don’t really consider what kind of people are going to be on this campus,” Hsu said. “I think it’s a debate on your morals, of whether you really care more about the prestige and the look of it.”
She said that these morals became especially important when deciding whether Cornell’s architecture program was worth reconsidering.
“You’re going to be going to a school that doesn’t support you beyond just having the classes you want,” Hsu said.
According to Hsu, safety concerns extend beyond campus boundaries. She considers whether she could walk alone at night, what it would be like to live in a single room, or a double room with others, and how the area surrounding a campus might affect her daily life.
During a recent tour of the University of Southern California, Hsu said she found herself considering not only the school’s facilities and opportunities, but also the streets and neighborhoods surrounding the Los Angeles campus.
Cornell isn’t the only campus where different approaches were undertaken with respect to reported sexual misconduct. At the University of Maryland, 278 reports of sex-based discrimination and harassment were filed with the university during the 2024-2025 academic year. Of those formal complaints, the university reported several expulsions, year-long suspensions, probation, and other dismissals and pending cases.
Cornell’s disciplinary data provides another point of comparison. More than 1,200 reports of sexual misconduct were made at Cornell between 2018 and 2024, according to a USA Today analysis. Of those, 162 resulted in disciplinary charges, and of those, 51 were in findings of responsibility, with seven expulsions or dismissals.
“Based on the information that I think everyone’s been given, it does not seem like the punishment was fit for the crime,” Massabki said.
Cornell has begun changing its approach following an internal investigation; they established a Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault in February 2025, with recommendations released in March 2026 focused on expanded prevention education and reporting options. The issues have also been addressed by lawmakers in New York, who are revisiting the state’s sexual assault laws, pushing for better distinction between voluntary and involuntary intoxication.
For now, though, high school and college students continue to wait for demonstrated changes in campus culture.
“I just feel that school should be a safe place, where everyone can belong and not be sexually assaulted,” Narth said.
